title: Efficient energy scavengers by flexible robot arm with non-uniform cross-section

sections.heading: Efficient energy scavengers by flexible robot arm with non-uniform cross-section
sections.text:
M. Do ˜gan

Department of Control Engineering, Dogus University, Acibadem, Kadikoy, 34722 Istanbul,Turkey E-mail: mdogan@dogus.edu.tr

Abstract: The vibration-based energy scavenger consists of beams with piezoelectric layers and proof mass, is usually designed by single-link or cantilever beam configurations. In order to overcome inherent problems, for example, insufficient bandwidth and model inaccuracies, we consider the motion of a two-link flexible arm with non-uniform cross-section. The governing equations consist of coupled non-linear partial differential equations (PDE) with appropriate boundary conditions. Most of the energy scavengers are based on linear electromechanical devices excited at resonance. Besides, realistic vibration environments can be described as stochastic, multi-frequency and time varying. Thus, narrow band linear systems could be highly inefficient under these conditions. On the contrary, non-linear systems are capable of responding over a broad frequency range and can have efficient performance in realistic vibration environments. The author shows that with the proposed non-linear-coupled set-up, the efficiency objectives are satisfied. In this research, tapered beam structure is exploited to achieve large bandwidth, tolerable excitation amplitude and maximum output power. The author also presents some simulation and experimental results to demonstrate the efficiency of proposed energy harvesting system. Consequently, the theoretical approach is verified by simulated and experimental results in compliance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The widespread application of portable electronic devices or wireless sensors cannot rely on power supplies with a limited lifespan. This idea motivated researchers in energy scavenging area and increased research on this problem. Power harvesting by using ambient motion, vibration sources, for example, trains, buildings, bridges, cars, aircraft, manufacturing tools, is a well-known and heuristically developed method. This method can be classified into three main focus areas: electrostatics, electromagnetic and piezoelectric materials that are able to interchange electrical energy and mechanical strain or force [1–4]. Owing to recent developments in micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) and wireless techniques, sensors/actuators can be used in remote and exotic locations. The power supply for these electronic devices is mostly the conventional battery with limited lifetime. These devices are usually hard to repair due to fact that they are normally embedded in probably inaccessible locations such as bridges, civil buildings, even human body. Therefore energy harvesting is indispensable for extending the lifetime of these devices [5–7].

In this research, piezoelectric materials surrounding the flexible beams will be used to capture the ambient motion.

However, the structural modelling of the flexible arms are much more complicated due to non-linear coupling between elastic and rigid modes during the complex manoeuvres especially with high angular velocities. Recognising this modelling challenge, we used the partial differential equations (PDE) approach which is known to yield more accurate results as compared to finite-dimensional, for example, ordinary differential equations (ODE) or finite element method (FEM), approaches, see for example [8, 9]. Therefore we will start with the infinite-dimensional model introduced in [8]. The goal of this study is to develop a non-linear-coupled model of the flexible energy harvesting device. This model would simplify the design procedure and extend the bandwidth necessary for sufficient energy to be produced.

In order to improve the important features of flexible links such as low mass, low moments of inertia and high natural frequencies, optimal shape design can be used, see for example [10]. Furthermore, a high fundamental frequency is desired since it implies a large bandwidth that will allow for fast motion without causing serious vibration problems, see for example [11]. In this paper, inspired by the approaches given in [8, 10, 11], we consider the motion of a two-link flexible arm with variable cross-section. We first present the equations of motion which are obtained by using the extended Hamilton’s principle. These equations are nonlinear and contain coupled PDEs and ODEs with appropriate boundary conditions.

The tapered beam structure and inherent non-linearity of the flexible arm model are important to achieve large bandwidth, maximum output power, robustness to external excitation goals. Hence, different from the most of the energy scavenging schemes proposed for cantilever beams with permanent magnets, see for example [12–17], we do not use magnets, multiple beam-mass systems and lumpedparameter models to improve the bandwidth and/or to introduce the non-linearity.

The proposed non-uniform link geometry provides efficient-large bandwidth and uniform strain field that result in resonating with different peak-power frequencies of various vibration sources. Also, the power spectrum is significantly enhanced by non-linear model, especially for low frequencies that covers the most of practical ambient vibrations. In this research, large and persistent vibrations are achieved by means of an accurate and sophisticated model. Besides, the experimental results indicated that the proposed model complied with in practice as well as in theory.

The two-link flexible arm configuration which is considered in this paper is shown in Fig. 1. Referring to Fig. 1, the various symbols represent the following; $X _ { o } Y _ { o }$ : global inertial system of coordinates; $X _ { 1 } Y _ { 1 }$ : body-fixed system of coordinates attached to undeformed link 1, $X _ { 2 } Y _ { 2 }$ body-fixed system of coordinates attached to undeformed link 2, $\theta _ { 1 } , \theta _ { 2 }$ : angular displacements of links 1 and 2, $w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 }$ flexural displacements of links 1 and 2.

This paper is organised as follows. In the next section, we present the equations of motion for the system shown in Fig. 1. In Section 3, we present our energy scavenger design. In Section 4, we present some simulation results which show the efficiency of the proposed system. In the following section, some important experimental results are presented for validation and in Section 6 we give some concluding remarks.

sections.heading: 2 Analytical model
sections.text:
The derived equations of motion for the system shown in Fig. 1 are obtained with the extended Hamilton’s principle, see for example [18] and extensive work in [8]. Since the ratio between the length of the beam and its thickness is sufficiently large as proposed in [18, 19], links can be modelled as Euler–Bernoulli beams, which can only be deformed in the flexural direction. Assuming that the manipulator moves in the horizontal plane, in the absence of gravity the potential energy depends only on the flexural deflections. sections.heading: 3 Energy scavenger design
sections.text:
Most of the energy scavengers are based on linear electromechanical devices excited at resonance. Besides, realistic vibration environments can be described as stochastic, multi-frequency and time varying. Thus, narrow band linear systems could be highly inefficient under these conditions. On the contrary, non-linear systems are capable of responding over a broad frequency range and can have efficient performance in realistic vibration environments. We show that with the proposed non-linear-coupled set-up, the efficiency objectives are satisfied in sequel.

Also, we propose a novel energy scavenger based on tapered geometry of the flexible arm, covered with thin piezoelectric materials. The system given by (1)–(9) are modified with damping terms and external excitation. Two types of damping mechanisms are introduced to the undamped arm model in [8]: viscous damping and Kelvin– Voigt (or strain-rate) damping. These terms are included in the model because of extreme sensitivity to mechanical damping for the power output under resonance excitation. Therefore designing the energy harvester beam to have less damping can be more important than choosing the right piezoelectric material [20]. Modified equations are given below

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle { \ddot { w } } _ { 1 } + \frac { ( E I _ { 1 } ( x _ { 1 } ) w _ { 1 x x } ) _ { x x } + ( S _ { f } I _ { 1 } ( x _ { 1 } ) \dot { w } _ { 1 x x } ) _ { x x } + V _ { f } \dot { w } _ { 1 } } { \rho _ { 1 } ( x _ { 1 } ) } } } \\ { ~ } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ = - \ddot { u } - x _ { 1 } \ddot { \theta } _ { 1 } } } \\ { { \displaystyle { \ddot { w } } _ { 2 } + \frac { ( E I _ { 2 } ( x _ { 2 } ) w _ { 2 x x } ) _ { x x } + ( S _ { f } I _ { 2 } ( x _ { 2 } ) \dot { w } _ { 2 x x } ) _ { x x } + V _ { f } \dot { w } _ { 2 } } { \rho _ { 2 } ( x _ { 2 } ) } } } \\ { ~ } \\ { { \displaystyle ~ + \cos \theta _ { 2 } \left[ \ddot { w } _ { 1 } ( l _ { 1 } , t ) + l _ { 1 } \ddot { \theta } _ { 1 } \right] } } \\ { { \displaystyle - \dot { \theta } _ { 2 } \sin \theta _ { 2 } \left[ \dot { w } _ { 1 } ( l _ { 1 } , t ) + l _ { 1 } \dot { \theta } _ { 1 } \right] = - a _ { \mathrm { u } } \ddot { u } - x _ { 2 } \ddot { \theta } _ { 2 } } } \end{array}

$$

Also, the operator $A$ generates a $C _ { 0 }$ semigroup $T ( t )$ in $\hat { \bf H }$ . It has been proven in [8] that $( \lambda I - A ) ^ { - 1 }$ is a compact operator on $\hat { \bf H }$ for sufficiently large $\lambda > 0$ , see for example [21]. Therefore the spectrum of $A$ consists only of isolated eigenvalues, which distribute in conjugate pairs on the complex plane, see for example [22, Lemma 2.1]. By introducing damping terms in this section, we need to define damping operator, $D$ such that $D = V _ { f } I + ( S _ { f } / E ) A _ { i }$ , where $I$ is identity operator and $A _ { i }$ operators in relevant Hilbert space as defined, see for example [8] and [23]. A few useful results on variable coefficient damping operators and their contribution to eigenvalues have been given in [22]. For undamped case, the asymptotic properties of eigenvalues are given below [22, Proposition 2.2]

$$

$$

where $n$ is large positive integer, $i = 1 , 2$ and $j = \sqrt { - 1 }$ . The periodic nature of corresponding eigenfunctions also depends on $n$ [22, Proposition 2.3]. The structure of $n$ -dependent terms in damped case does not change significantly such that $( n + 1 / 2 ) ( \pi / h )$ for linearly tapered links, see for example [22, Proposition 2.10]. Besides, (14) has a unique local solution $\mathbf { z } ( \cdot )$ , which is implicitly given below [24, Theorem 2]

$$
\mathbf { z } ( t ) = T ( t ) \mathbf { z } ( 0 ) + \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } T ( t - s ) f ( \mathbf { z } ( s ) ) \mathrm { d } s , \quad t \geq 0
$$

where $T ( t )$ is the semigroup generated by $A$ and $f$ represents a non-linear operator. Thus, we can conclude that the vibration modes will be enriched and distributed over the broad frequency range due to non-linear coupling in (16).

We also note that in this work we mainly consider nonuniform cross-sections for the flexible links. Despite the fact that such links have some advantages over uniform links, they are seldom considered in the literature due to the resulting theoretical difficulties. One important reason to utilise non-uniform flexible link is the fact that it increases the system bandwidth, see for example [10, 11]. As a consequence, this may increase the scavenger performance, for example, it may result in resonating

with different peak-power frequencies of various vibration sources. Besides, research on energy harvesting prove that tapered beam geometry provides uniform strain field, for example, trapezoidal geometry can supply efficiently more than twice the energy per unit volume than the rectangular one [25]. Also, increasing the slope of tapering improves bandwidth [26, 27]. Recently, Paquin and St-Amant [28], who achieved a substantial increase of the harvested power by almost a factor of four by using variable beam geometry, for example, tapered single beam. In this research, different from the last approach, flexible arm model is used to introduce non-linearity and model validation has been elaborated with the PDE method instead of FEM.

Compared with our infinite-dimensional model, lumpedparameter models might have intolerable-large modelling errors due to the fact that they ignore the contribution of the relatively large distributed inertia to the excitation amplitude [20]. On the other hand, developed non-linearcoupled model are capable of responding over a broad frequency range and can have robust performance in realistic vibration environments. The proposed flexible energy harvesting device can be easily implemented owing to its simple geometry and structure.

sections.heading: 4 Simulation results
sections.text:
The proposed scheme is tested with the simulation program implemented in MATLAB. The PDEs are discretised in the space domain by the finite difference method to obtain ODEs at each of the nodes. Then, ODEs are solved numerically. Instead of dealing with complexity of the fourth-order derivative approximation, the second-order derivative approximation has been used with the help of auxiliary states. Those states are more meaningful in a real problem as well since they corresponds to physical variables such as deflections, velocity and bending moments, see for example [29]. However, the number of ODEs to solve and the computation time are increased in return of the robust stability of the numerical scheme. sections.heading: 5 Experimental results
sections.text:
The most well-known piezoelectric transducer, PZT (mostly consists of lead, zirconate and titanate), was developed at the Tokyo Institute of Technology in the 1950s and various versions of this material are widely used for many engineering applications. For example, piezoelectric diaphragms (buzzers) are commonly used as basic electronic sound components with the advantages of simple structure, stable performance and high reliability. In the mean time, they also used as shock sensors in many sensitive equipments.

sections.text:
piezoelectric materials were placed on two opposite sides of the links in multiple configuration. The experimental setup used for measurements is shown in Fig. 6. Ambient vibration is provided with adjustable electronic shaker (MIKROTEK Dental Shaker RC - 402) and measured by digital storage oscilloscope (RIGOL DS 5202MA, Two Channel, 200 MHz, 1 GS/s). Flexible beams are clamped to the shaker frame for persistent base excitation. The second link is configured to freely rotate with an attached tip mass $( 0 . 0 2 \mathrm { k g } )$ . Digital oscilloscope is directly connected to data acquisition/analyser system, which is actually a personal computer (PC) without any amplification. For frequency responses, built-in fast Fourier transform (FFT) function of the oscilloscope has been used. All figures in this section except the first one, are oscilloscope images.

Time response of the single link 1 with tip mass is obviously unimodal frequency spectrum, see Fig. 7 and this linear system behaviour is observed for different level of external vibrations. However, time responses of the flexible arm with tip mass in Figs. 8–12 are similar to white noise with quite high peak-to-peak voltage values without amplification. This multi-modal nature of the harvested signal can be observed at frequency responses in Figs. 13–18 as well. The frequency value at upper right of all related figures is just an estimation of dominant frequency. Variation of this value throughout the all figures and also rich content of the frequency spectrum in Figs. 13–18 prove that multi-modal behaviour or broad frequency spectrum have been obtained by non-linear-coupled model and design. Note that estimated frequency value in Fig. 17 is quite high as expected due to reduced tip mass. For Figs. 17 and 18, we removed the regular tip mass and left only the link 2 as fixed tip mass with reduction ratio about 2/3. All measurements have been taken from the bottom piezo transducer of the link 1. Other transducers gave the similar results. In future, all transducers can be connected together with the most efficient configuration and energy storage circuit.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusions
sections.text:
In this paper, we considered both the modelling and the design of energy scavenger by a two-link flexible arm with variable cross-section. The physical configuration which we considered is given in Fig. 1. For the modelling, we used PDE approach which is known to yield more accurate results as compared to finite dimensional, for example, ODE, FEM, approaches.

It has been shown by the simulation results that the new design method can provide efficient energy scavenging without complex structures. Non-linearity and coupled dynamics of flexible arm exploited to enrich the power spectrum content especially for low frequencies that covers most of the practical ambient vibrations. The shape of the power spectrum is retained effectively even with some geometry and mass changes. This proves the robustness of the proposed scheme. The tapered beam structure and inherent non-linearity of the flexible arm model are important to achieve large bandwidth, maximum output power, robustness to external excitation goals. We also present some experimental results to demonstrate the performance of the proposed energy harvesting system. Time and frequency histories of the vibration modes prove the efficiency of the non-linear-coupled design. In this research, the theoretical approach is verified by simulated and experimental results in compliance.
